# Media fixtures — provenance record

Golden fixtures for the M2 C2PA check (`src/markproof/checks/c2pa_verify.py`).
They exist to separate two questions that are easy to conflate: whether an
asset carries a sound C2PA manifest, and whether that manifest actually
asserts `digitalSourceType = trainedAlgorithmicMedia`, which is what turns a
signature into an EU AI Act Art. 50 disclosure. Several fixtures below answer
the first question with a confident yes and the second with a no — those are
the ones that matter, because a check that stops at signature verification
passes them and is wrong.

Everything here is generated by [`generate.py`](generate.py) and inventoried
in [`MANIFEST.json`](MANIFEST.json).

## Hard rule (Auflage H2): every asset is our own production

No third-party media enters this directory — not a stock photo, not a sample
clip, not a "harmless" example image from the web. The images, the audio and
the video frames are synthesised from closed-form integer expressions inside
`generate.py`:

- **Images** come from `_pixel(x, y)`, a pure function producing a diagonal RGB
  gradient with a dark border and an inverted centre block.
- **Audio** is an integer triangle wave (~444 Hz at 8 kHz) with a short fade to
  avoid clicks.
- **Video** is five of our own JPEG frames with the pattern phase-shifted per
  frame, muxed as Motion JPEG.

Nothing is downloaded and nothing is copied. The encoders are written from
scratch in `generate.py` too — there is no Pillow, no ffmpeg and no `c2patool`
in the chain, only the standard library plus `c2pa-python` for signing.

## Test signing material — NOT FOR PRODUCTION

`generate.py` embeds an ECDSA P-256 private key and a self-signed CA chain in
plain text. **This is deliberate and it is safe, but only because:**

- the root CA is self-signed and appears in no trust store anywhere;
- markproof never trusts it at runtime — the tests inject it as an explicit
  C2PA trust anchor and nothing else does;
- the certificate subject reads `NOT FOR PRODUCTION` in the OU field.

**Never reuse this key to sign anything real.** Any manifest signed with it is
worthless as provenance evidence by construction. If you need a fresh chain
(the current one expires 2036-01-01), run `python generate.py
--regenerate-test-certs` and paste the output back into the constants.

The root CA alone is also published in `MANIFEST.json` under
`signing.trust_anchor_pem`, so tests can configure trust without parsing the
generator. It is a public certificate; nothing about it is secret.

## The matrix

Four states across four formats, plus three PNG-only edge cases — 19 files.
`state` is the value in `MANIFEST.json`; "must" describes what the Art. 50
check should conclude.

| File | State | C2PA validation | `digitalSourceType` | Art. 50 verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `signed-valid.{png,jpg,mp4,wav}` | `signed-valid` | `Trusted` | `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` | **must PASS** |
| `signed-wrong-type.{png,jpg,mp4,wav}` | `signed-wrong-type` | `Trusted` | `algorithmicMedia` | **must FAIL** |
| `unsigned.{png,jpg,mp4,wav}` | `unsigned` | no manifest (raises) | — | must FAIL |
| `tampered.{png,jpg,mp4,wav}` | `tampered` | `Invalid` | `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` | must FAIL |
| `signed-wrong-type-capture.png` | `signed-wrong-type` | `Trusted` | `digitalCapture` | must FAIL |
| `signed-composite.png` | `signed-edge-case` | `Trusted` | `compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia` | policy call |
| `signed-no-source-type.png` | `signed-no-source-type` | `Trusted` | *(absent)* | must FAIL |

A few of these deserve explanation.

**`signed-wrong-type` is the important one.** It is signed by the same CA, the
hash binding is intact, and it validates as `Trusted` with zero failures. The
only thing wrong with it is one entry in the IPTC vocabulary:
`algorithmicMedia` means rule-based or procedural output — a Perlin-noise
texture, a fractal — not the output of a trained model. It is one vocabulary
step from compliant and carries no cryptographic signal at all, which is
exactly why assertion-level checking is the point of M2.

**`tampered` inverts the trap.** The manifest still asserts
`trainedAlgorithmicMedia` and the claim signature still verifies; only the
content hash no longer matches. Reading the assertion without checking the
validation state passes this one.

**`signed-composite.png` has no obviously correct answer.** Art. 50(2) reaches
content that is generated *or manipulated*, so a human-authored composite
containing AI-generated regions may well require disclosure. The fixture is
here to force the check to take an explicit position rather than fall through
to a default.

**`signed-no-source-type.png` is a trusted manifest that says nothing about AI
provenance** — the shape older or minimal signers emit. It must fail the Art. 50
check without being misreported as a broken signature.

## What worked, and what to know before writing the check

All four formats sign, verify and tamper-detect correctly. Nothing was dropped.

| Format | Signs | Validates | Tamper detected as | Independent decoder check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PNG | yes | `Trusted` | `assertion.dataHash.mismatch` | macOS ImageIO (`sips`), 64×64 |
| JPEG | yes | `Trusted` | `assertion.dataHash.mismatch` | macOS ImageIO (`sips`), 64×64 |
| WAV | yes | `Trusted` | `assertion.dataHash.mismatch` | `afinfo`, 1 ch / 8 kHz / Int16 |
| MP4 | yes | `Trusted` | `assertion.bmffHash.mismatch` | `ffmpeg` full decode, 0 errors; `ffprobe` reports `mjpeg 64×64`, 5 frames, 1.0 s |

Note that MP4 fails with `assertion.bmffHash.mismatch`, not
`assertion.dataHash.mismatch` — ISO-BMFF uses a different hash assertion, so a
check that matches on the `dataHash` code alone will miss tampered video.

Four findings from building these are worth carrying into the check:

**`Reader.is_valid` is not a validation result.** It is a resource-liveness
property inherited from `ManagedResource` and reports whether the Reader is
still open. It returns `True` for every tampered fixture here. Use
`get_validation_state()` and `get_validation_results()` instead.

**Unsigned media raises rather than returning.** `c2pa.Reader` throws
`ManifestNotFound` when there is no JUMBF data, so "no provenance" arrives as
an exception, not as a falsy state. The `unsigned.*` fixtures cover this.

**Trust is configured, not inherent.** Without an explicit trust anchor a
correctly signed fixture validates as `Valid` with the failure
`signingCredential.untrusted`; with `signing.trust_anchor_pem` injected it
reaches `Trusted` with no failures. Both are worth testing — real endpoints
often serve certificates the runtime does not trust, and that is a different
finding from a missing or wrong assertion.

```python
settings = c2pa.Settings.from_dict({
    "verify": {"verify_trust": True},
    "trust": {"trust_anchors": root_ca_pem},   # MANIFEST.json -> signing.trust_anchor_pem
})
reader = c2pa.Reader(path, context=c2pa.ContextBuilder().with_settings(settings).build())
```

**c2pa-rs 0.90.15 refuses to emit `c2pa.created` without a
`digitalSourceType` at claim v2**, rejecting it as
`assertion.action.malformed`. `signed-no-source-type.png` therefore uses
`claim_version: 1`, which the SDK accepts. The check must still handle the
missing field defensively: other producers are not bound by this SDK's
validation rules.

Thumbnails are disabled in the builder. They roughly tripled fixture size
(74 KB against 26 KB for a signed PNG) without adding anything at assertion
level. One consequence to keep in mind: were they enabled, a signed JPEG would
contain a *second* JPEG before the primary image, which is precisely the trap
`jpeg_primary_dqt_offset()` in `generate.py` walks the marker segments to
avoid.

## Regenerating

```sh
.venv-dev/bin/python tests/fixtures/media/generate.py            # fill in what is missing
.venv-dev/bin/python tests/fixtures/media/generate.py --force    # re-sign everything
.venv-dev/bin/python tests/fixtures/media/generate.py --verify   # check only, write nothing
```

Every run reads each fixture back through `c2pa.Reader` and asserts that its
validation state, failure codes and `digitalSourceType` match what its name
claims, printing a per-file table and exiting non-zero on any mismatch. A
fixture that is not what its filename says is worse than no fixture, so this
check is not optional — `--verify` is cheap enough to run in CI.

The default run is idempotent: it only creates files that are missing, so
re-running leaves the working tree untouched and `git status` clean.

## Reproducibility, honestly

**Base (unsigned) media are bit-exact reproducible**, and `MANIFEST.json`
carries their SHA-256. This holds across platforms, not just across runs on one
machine: the PNG uses stored (uncompressed) DEFLATE blocks so no zlib version
can change the bytes, the JPEG encoder runs an all-integer DCT with a cosine
table rounded to 14 bits (far coarser than any libm's error), the colour
conversion uses fixed-point integer coefficients, and the audio is integer
arithmetic throughout. No timestamp and no RNG reaches the output.

**Signed media are not byte-reproducible, and cannot be.** An ECDSA signature
embeds a fresh random nonce on every run and c2pa mints a new manifest UUID
each time, so the bytes differ even though the content does not. Pinning a hash
for them would guarantee a false alarm. `MANIFEST.json` therefore records
`"sha256": null` for every signed asset, with `sha256_note` giving the reason,
and pins their **properties** instead — `expected_validation_state`,
`expected_failure_codes`, `expected_source_type`,
`expected_manifest_present`. Those are stable, and they are what the tests
should assert.

Verified by running the generator twice: a default second run left all 19
files and `MANIFEST.json` byte-identical, and a `--force` run left the four
base media and `MANIFEST.json` byte-identical while re-signing the other 15.
`MANIFEST.json` is itself stable because it contains no timestamp and no hash
of a signed file.

## Inventory

Sizes are from the current generation; signed sizes may shift by a byte or two
between runs as DER-encoded signature lengths vary.

| File | Format | Bytes | Generated by | Signed with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `unsigned.png` | PNG, 64×64 RGB8 | 12,420 | `make_png()` | — |
| `unsigned.jpg` | JPEG baseline 4:4:4 q80 | 2,179 | `make_jpeg()` | — |
| `unsigned.mp4` | ISO-BMFF / Motion JPEG, 5 frames | 11,539 | `make_mp4()` | — |
| `unsigned.wav` | RIFF PCM s16le mono 8 kHz | 16,044 | `make_wav()` | — |
| `signed-valid.png` | PNG | 25,759 | `make_png()` + sign | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-valid.jpg` | JPEG | 15,518 | `make_jpeg()` + sign | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-valid.mp4` | MP4 | 24,988 | `make_mp4()` + sign | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-valid.wav` | WAV | 29,380 | `make_wav()` + sign | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-wrong-type.png` | PNG | 25,757 | as above, `algorithmicMedia` | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-wrong-type.jpg` | JPEG | 15,516 | as above, `algorithmicMedia` | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-wrong-type.mp4` | MP4 | 24,986 | as above, `algorithmicMedia` | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-wrong-type.wav` | WAV | 29,378 | as above, `algorithmicMedia` | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-wrong-type-capture.png` | PNG | 25,764 | as above, `digitalCapture` | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-composite.png` | PNG | 25,776 | as above, `compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia` | test CA, ES256 |
| `signed-no-source-type.png` | PNG | 25,710 | as above, no `digitalSourceType`, claim v1 | test CA, ES256 |
| `tampered.png` | PNG | 25,758 | sign, then invert a 16-row pixel band | test CA, ES256 |
| `tampered.jpg` | JPEG | 15,517 | sign, then rewrite primary DQT coefficients | test CA, ES256 |
| `tampered.mp4` | MP4 | 24,987 | sign, then patch DQT inside `mdat` | test CA, ES256 |
| `tampered.wav` | WAV | 29,380 | sign, then offset 400 PCM samples | test CA, ES256 |

Every tampered fixture is patched through a structural walk of its container —
PNG chunks, JPEG marker segments, RIFF chunks, ISO-BMFF boxes — so the file
stays well-formed and still decodes; only the C2PA hash binding breaks. The
changes are real content changes, not cosmetic byte flips: `tampered.png`
differs from `signed-valid.png` in 24.9 % of decoded scanline bytes, and the
JPEG, MP4 and WAV cases were confirmed by decoding both versions and comparing
the output.
